10852-hardy-ornamental-flowering-trees-a:
A. D. Webster, author of Practical Forestry and British Orchids, published Hardy Ornamental Flowering Trees and Shrubs in 1897, from a first edition of 1893. His preface protests the dull repetition in parks and gardens of elm, lime, and oak, with cherry laurel and privet for shrubs. A host of choice flowering kinds, he argues, are just as hardy and far more beautiful.

Webster describes species of the simplest culture, suited to public and private grounds. His book aims to widen planters' choices beyond the familiar few. Gardeners get a practical Victorian guide, still useful for finding hardy flowers among trees and shrubs.
11416-a-description-of-modern-birmingham:
Charles Pye's Description of Modern Birmingham, with observations from an excursion round the town in summer 1818, including Warwick and Leamington, surveys the factory town as a visitor found it. Pye, compiler of a Dictionary of Ancient Geography praised for clear arrangement of ancient and modern names, turns the same careful eye to modern streets, trades, and buildings. The excursion format lets him compare Birmingham with neighboring spa and county towns.

The book's value is local: Birmingham on the eve of its great Victorian expansion, described by a contemporary gazetteer-maker. For urban historians, it preserves workshops, streets, and suburbs before railways and town rebuilding transformed them.
16923-a-handbook-for-latin-clubs:
Susan Paxson, teacher of Latin at Central High School in Omaha, wrote this 1916 handbook for Latin clubs, issued by D. C. Heath in Boston, New York, and Chicago. Programs run from the value of Latin and Pompeii into ancient Rome. The forum, the house, slaves, children, and schools follow. Trades, doctors, soldiers, Caesar, Cicero, Vergil, and Horace appear too. Holidays, funerals, games, buildings, letters, gods, and a Roman banquet close the set.

Paxson gives each program in short, usable form, with songs marked for music in the html edition. The book helps a club stage a Roman evening, a talk, or a play with little fuss. Modern Latin teachers and students will still find it a handy source of program ideas, and a window on how 1916 schools made Rome live.
17278-the-women-of-the-arabs:
Henry Harris Jessup's 1873 Women of the Arabs, with a chapter for children, draws on seventeen years as an American missionary in Syria. Chapters treat women in the Jahiliyeh, or times of ignorance, women in the Mohammedan world, Druze and Nusairiyeh women, women's work from 1820 to 1872, Mrs. Whiting's school, Dr. De Forest's work in Beirut, and modern Syrian views on female education. A Mount Lebanon proverb on a girl's birth heads the book.

Jessup writes in earnest missionary prose, with Beiruit schools and Syrian homes in plain detail. The book suits historians of missions, education, and the Levant. As a period document, it shows both sympathy and the limits of its age, and should be read with that frame in mind.
22605-book-lovers-bibliomaniacs-and-book:
Book Lovers, Bibliomaniacs and Book Clubs is an essay collection about the love of books and the people who collect them. The catalog record names no author and gives no year. It traces how book collecting, once a hobby of the rich, spread to people of moderate means.

Each generation of collectors, the author notes, has outnumbered the one before in both numbers and enthusiasm. The love of books creeps quietly into homes grand and humble, since a library counts as equipment for the mind as much as for the house. Clubs, sales, and famous collections fill the pages. The book is a friendly tour of bibliophile culture, written for readers who already suspect books are more than objects.
24610-dumpy-proverbs: Honor C. Appleton compiled this tiny picture book, number 24 in the Dumpy Books for Children. Each page pairs a familiar proverb with a picture. They include conscience makes cowards of us all, time and tide wait for no man, and fine feathers make fine birds. Others are look before you leap, pride comes before a fall, a stitch in time saves nine, and where there's a will there's a way.
24680-the-martyr-of-the-catacombs:
Published at New York and Cincinnati with illustrations, this tale of ancient Rome follows Christians hiding in the catacombs under persecution. Its chapters run from the Coliseum, the Praetorian camp, and the Appian Way to the catacombs themselves, the Christian's secret, and the cloud of witnesses.

Later chapters tell of life in the catacombs, the persecution, the arrest, the offer, Pollio's trial and death, and the temptation of Lucullus. A plan of the catacombs and a picture of the boy martyr accompany the text. Readers get a vivid, earnest story of faith under Rome, in the style of Victorian Christian romance.
2686-the-book-of-snobs:
William Makepeace Thackeray, calling himself One of Themselves, wrote this anatomy of snobs, with prefatory remarks on why such a work was needed. History, he argues, has been preparing the world for the work and the man, and snobs must be studied like other objects of natural science.

Thackeray marches through clubs, colleges, courts, and country houses, naming snobbery in every rank. His satire is sharp, funny, and uncomfortably personal, since he counts himself among the tribe. The book remains a classic of English humor, and a mirror that still catches readers.
314-guide-to-life-and-literature-of-the-:
J. Frank Dobie invites anybody to help himself to this guide, free of copyright in 1942 and 1952. His Guide to Life and Literature of the Southwest, revised and enlarged for Southern Methodist University Press, surveys a region's books and ways. A preface with revised ideas opens.

Chapters run from interpreters of the land through Indian cultures, Spanish-Mexican strains, and backwoods humor. Texas Rangers, women pioneers, circuit riders, and cowboys follow, with Santa Fe trails and stagecoaches. Dobie lists the books that best tell each life. The guide remains a Southwest classic.
31943-leonore-stubbs:
L. B. Walford's 1908 novel Leonore Stubbs, published by Longmans, Green and Company, opens with a quarrel between General Boldero and his eldest daughter Sukey over Leonore. The general insists she has no settlement, damn it, and shall not come, while Sukey holds a black-edged letter that is the apple of discord between them.

The general says he was cheated and swindled: he married his daughter to a rich man, who died and left her a pauper. Chapters follow a station platform, speculations, old playmates meeting, a revelation, and a cat-and-mouse game. Readers get an Edwardian society novel of money, marriage, and family pride.
34012-labor-and-freedom-the-voice-and-pe:
Eugene V. Debs speaks in this collection of voice and pen, published at Saint Louis in 1916 by Phil Wagner. An introduction recalls the tale of the old umbrella mender, first read in manuscript, as the piece that best shows Debs's tender heart and rare mind. The writer calls every line a treasure and every sentiment an appeal to justice, equality, and freedom.

Debs's speeches and writings in the set take up labor, class, prison, and the soul's freedom. The book preserves the voice of America's best-known socialist orator. It serves readers who want Debs in his own words, plain and passionate.
35992-memoirs-of-orange-jacobs:
Orange Jacobs wrote his own memoirs at the age of eighty, and Lowman and Hanford published them at Seattle in 1908. He was born in the Genesee Valley of New York on May 2, 1827, the second of eight children. His mother rules the early pages: a woman of round-about common sense whose governing power was affection. Certainty, not severity, was her rule of punishment, and her sons obeyed her because they loved her.

The contents carry him west. He crossed the plains in 1852 and spent fifty-six years in Oregon and Washington. Pen sketches of pioneer life fill the middle of the book. Further chapters treat Indian civilization and its true methods, Indian customs, legends, and philosophy. Official life, public addresses, and the game animals and birds of Washington follow. Jacobs dedicated the book to the pioneers of the state, whose labours gave Washington to the Union.
36875-midnight-webs:
George Fenn wrote these tales, published by Tinsley Brothers in London in an edition of 1872. Smith's Ditty is the first story, with an introduction of first words at its head. The narrator has waited many years for someone to give a true account, he begins in that story.

Seeing other parts and other people's sufferings told, while ours never got a line, stirred him. Fairness is what he always liked, he says, and he sets to against his will. His empty sleeve keeps the paper from sitting straight as he writes, a veteran's quiet sign that these midnight webs are tales of the Indian Mutiny years.
37985-a-literary-history-of-the-arabs:
A literary history of the Arabs by Reynold A Nicholson. T Fisher Unwin published the first edition in 1907. Cambridge University Press reprinted it for decades, this copy in 1966. A manuscript miniature of litigants before a judge fronts the book. It comes from a 1256 copy of Hariri's Maqamat. Nicholson dedicates the work to Professor A A Bevan.

Saba and Himyar open the story in ancient Yemen. Pagan Arab history, legends, poetry, and religion follow. The Prophet and the Koran anchor the fourth chapter. Orthodox and Umayyad caliphates carry literature into empire. Baghdad's Abbasid age gets two chapters of poetry and science. Orthodoxy, free thought, and mysticism contend in the eighth. Nicholson, Cambridge's great Arabist, made the survey a classic.
42189-the-expositor-s-bible-the-book-of-:
Horton wrote The Book of Proverbs for The Expositor's Bible, a series of commentaries edited by Robertson Nicoll, editor of The Expositor. Hodder and Stoughton of London published the series in crown octavo volumes at seven shillings and sixpence each. The Proverbs volume is dated 1890.

The series list at the front shows the plan: book by book through the Bible, each volume by a named scholar. Maclaren took Colossians, Marcus Dods Genesis and First Corinthians, and Smith the two halves of Isaiah. Judges and Ruth, Jeremiah, Exodus, and the Gospels stand in the later series. Horton's volume treats the wisdom book of the Old Testament, the proverbs of Solomon, in the same expository manner. Preachers and Bible students of the 1890s built whole shelves of these volumes, and Proverbs gave them the practical wisdom of the Bible chapter by chapter.
42999-old-boston-taverns-and-tavern-club:
Old Boston Taverns and Tavern Clubs, by Samuel Adams Drake, was issued at Boston in a new illustrated edition in 1917. A portrait of Captain John Marston fronts the book. Marston kept the Golden Ball and the Bunch of Grapes taverns in old Boston. An account of Cole’s Inn and the Bakers’ Arms comes from Watkins.

A list of taverns closes the added matter of the edition. That list gives the owners of each tavern property across the years. It draws on a work on the inhabitants and estates of Boston from 1630 to 1800. The foreword says the inns of old Boston played a great part in its history. Clubs met, news spread, and plots were laid in those rooms. Drake recovers a Boston of signs, landlords, and long evenings.
43267-captured-by-the-arabs:
James Foster wrote a boys' tale of the Sahara for Burt of New York, copyrighted in 1933. Chapter one opens on the deck of the steamer Sylvania. Joe Lewis and Bob Holton breathe the one word: adventure. Their first sight of North Africa is near.

An archaeologist named Kirshner smiles at their heat. He says the spirit came from their Brazil trip. The contents promise the true fare of the set. The party crosses the desert, fights heavy odds, and suffers thirst. Capture comes in its turn. A cave of treasure waits near the end, then the road back to settled lands.
44089-a-dissertation-on-the-inutility-of:
Bilguer, surgeon general to the armies of the King of Prussia, argues against cutting off limbs in a Latin work now Englished in 1764. Baldwin printed the London translation, with notes added by Tissot, a physician at Lausanne. An English surgeon, unnamed, made the translation and wrote a warm opening note.

The translator hopes the book will check a cruel and hasty practice of removing limbs that could be saved. He dedicates it to Pringle, whose work on diseases of the army set a standard for army doctors. Tissot and other judges praised Bilguer's modesty and candour, the note says. Readers are also told that a translation of Tissot on the people's health will soon appear.
44843-the-book-of-bulbs:
Arnott, a fellow of the Royal Horticultural Society, wrote this guide to bulb growing. Lane printed The Book of Bulbs in 1901, as the fifth of the Handbooks of Practical Gardening. Harry Roberts edited the line and wrote a first chapter on the science of bulbs.

Concerning Bulbs opens the book, then worth, use in grass, and beds in order. Bulbs for cutting, breeding more, and the ills of bulbs take their turns. Hardy bulbs then march by name: aconitums, alliums, and anemones first. Amaryllises, arums, camassias, and colchicums fill the next lists. Early tulips head the plates, in a book made for the working gardener.
44866-gombo-zhe-bes-little-dictionary-of:
Lafcadio Hearn gathers sayings in Gombo Zhebes, a little dictionary of Creole proverbs, printed in New York in 1885. Coleman made the book. The proverbs are drawn from six Creole dialects. They are rendered into French and into English, with notes and a full index to subjects. Brief remarks on the Creole idioms of Louisiana close the frame.

His first word plays on the dish that names the book. Any one who has paid a flying visit to New Orleans knows the gombo pots, he says. They are compounded of many odds and ends, with the okra plant for a basis. Gombo aux herbes, in an old cook's speech, is gombo zhebes. The folk sayings get the same rich, mixed treatment.
45442-a-camera-actress-in-the-wilds-of-t:
Gehrts wrote this account of her work as a camera actress in the wilds of Togoland, printed at Philadelphia and London in 1915, with 65 pictures and a map. An introduction by Major Schomburgk, the leader of the expedition, stands at the front. A frontispiece in words describes a Konkombwa warrior in full gala dress, with a helmet of calabash worked with cowrie shells.

The contents tell the trip in detail. Chapter one takes her from London to Lome, through doubts about a queer business offer to the start from England. Chapter two shows the filming of a drama, The White Goddess of the Wangora, from her hut in the forest to her bout of malarial fever. Life at Kamina follows.
49694-the-duke-in-the-suburbs:
The Duke in the Suburbs is a novel by Edgar Wallace. Wallace had written the Four Just Men and the Council of Justice before it. Ward Lock brought the book out in London in 1909. Wallace opens with an apology for his own trade as a maker of tales. He sets the scene in Brockley, a quiet London suburb, he says.

A duke, his friend Hank, a Mr Nape, and Big Bill Slewer fill the cast. Big Bill hails from Four Ways in Texas, far from Brockley streets. Miss Alicia Terrill of The Ferns stands last but not least in that list. Wallace plays the clash between high rank and plain home life. Court scenes in old Milan were easy to fake, he warns the reader. Plain folk in modern dress give the teller a far harder task.
52551-the-art-of-preserving-all-kinds-of:
Appert published 'The Art of Preserving All Kinds of Animal and Vegetable Substances for Several Years' by order of the French Minister of the Interior. This second English edition appeared in London in 1812. Front matter carries the minister's letter and the certificate of the Board of Arts and Manufactures. Early sections describe Appert's rooms, his bottles and vessels, his corks, and the art of corking itself.

The process then takes food by food: boiled meat, gravy, broth, fowls, new-laid eggs, milk, and cream. Vegetables follow in order, green peas, asparagus, Windsor beans, artichokes, cauliflowers, and sorrel, then fruits from currants and cherries to apricots, peaches, and pears. A closing part explains how to use what has been preserved, in soups, jellies, cordials, and ices.
55473-kotto-being-japanese-curios-with-s:
Lafcadio Hearn collected this book of Japanese tales and short pieces, printed in New York in 1903. Hearn taught literature at the Imperial University in Tokyo, and Genjiro Yeto drew the pictures. The title page calls the contents curios with sundry cobwebs. The book is given to Sir Edwin Arnold, in thanks for kind words.

The first part, Old Stories, holds nine tales drawn from old Japanese books. Hearn says they were picked to show strange beliefs. Later parts mix a woman's diary with short pieces on crabs, fireflies, dreams, and night thoughts. The first tale tells of Yurei-Daki, the Cascade of Ghosts, near the village of Kurosaka.
55739-artificial-limbs:
Artificial Limbs is a medical manual issued in 1918 in the Military Medical Manuals series. The authors are Broca, a Paris professor of anatomy, and Ducroquet, a surgeon in Paris. Their French text was translated and edited by Elmslie. He was a surgeon at a London hospital and at Roehampton. The book carries 208 illustrations. It came out in London and Paris in the last year of the Great War.

The manual deals with the fitting and use of false limbs. Its readers were surgeons and fitters who served maimed soldiers. The war had left great numbers of men with lost arms and legs. Sound fitting of a new limb shaped a man's return to work. The series set out to spread French war medicine in English. This volume gave British and American staff the French craft in full.
58791-precepts-in-practice-or-stories-il:
Stories that each act out a saying from the Book of Proverbs fill a volume printed in 1887 with thirty nine engravings. The author signed with the initials A L O E and had written The Silver Casket and The Robbers' Cave. In a preface to young friends, she says each tale shows a truth taught by Solomon. She hopes the holy words will stick once seen in daily life.

Tales include The Two Sons, The Prisoner Released, The Mother's Return, and The Friend in Need. Forbidden Ground and later stories keep the same pattern. The book turns short wise sayings into scenes a child might meet at home.
59164-index-of-the-project-gutenberg-wor:
David Widger built this index as a key to the Project Gutenberg texts of George Gibbs, the once famed teller of romantic tales. It lists his novels held there, from Paradise Garden and The Secret Witness to The Vagrant Duke and The Yellow Dove. Each entry gives the full table of contents of the book.

Readers can thus see a whole plot's frame at a glance, chapter by chapter, before they open the tale. Gibbs wrote spy tales of the Great War, sea stories, and tales of old France. The index is a finding aid, not a tale itself: a map of one popular author's shelf in the Gutenberg stacks.
59233-scarabs:
Scarabs is a study of Egyptian seals and signet rings by Percy E Newberry, issued in London in 1908 as a cheaper re-issue under the University of Liverpool's Institute of Archaeology. Newberry wrote The Amherst Papyri and The Life of Rekhmara, and he fills the book with forty-four plates and one hundred sixteen text illustrations.

His preface says the want of a full work on scarabs had been felt since Professor Flinders Petrie's Historical Scarabs went out of print in 1895. The first plate shows rings bearing the names of King Apepy, Nefer-Ka-Ra, Amenhetep II, Akhenaten, and Hor-em-heb. Newberry also notes that living near the Egyptian scarab market gave him unusual chances to study genuine pieces and modern imitations alike.
60050-the-book-of-herbs:
Lady Rosalind Northcote wrote The Book of Herbs, a hand book put out in London and New York in 1903. It is book twelve in a set of hand books on the work of gardens. Harry Roberts put that set in order. A plate shows John Parkinson, from a statue in Sefton Park at Liverpool.

A first part deals with the cries of street sellers in old London. The main part then treats the chief herbs in use in this day. Anise, balm, and two kinds of basil lead the list of plants. Borage, chervil, chives, and the seed called coriander follow. Cress, dandelion, dill, fennel, and horse-radish fill the midst of the list. Mint, mustard, parsley, sage, thyme, and tarragon close the roll. Each herb gets its past, its use at table, and its care in the ground.
60228-studies-in-life-from-jewish-prover:
W A L Elmslie, fellow of Christ's College, Cambridge, draws lessons in Studies in Life from Jewish Proverbs, published at London by James Clarke and Company. Twenty chapters move from the characteristics of proverbs and the proverbs of the Jews through forgotten years, the day of small things and iron sharpening iron, to wisdom's treasury, conduct and faith. The last chapter is called The Gift of God.

Elmslie opens with Lord Russell's epigram calling a proverb the wisdom of many and the wit of one. A saying becomes a proverb, he argues, only when many men commend it and it survives on the lips of the people.
6052-the-minds-and-manners-of-wild-anima:
William T. Hornaday, director of the New York Zoological Park, writes from personal observation that the wild animal must think, or die. His frontispiece shows a mountain sheep, a lava ram, standing spellbound on a lava crest in the Pinacate Mountains for twenty minutes, gazing at two men and a pack mule.

Chapters survey the field, the lay of the land, and wild animal temperament, drawing on years among zoo and field animals. Hornaday dedicates the book to the officers and men of the park, whose safety depends on knowing animal minds. The work argues that curiosity, temper, and habit shape survival.
6140-army-boys-on-german-soil-our-doughb:
Homer Randall sends his Army Boys onto German soil, where doughboys quell the mobs after the Great War. Chapters promise a flash from the guns, mystery, a storm, a ruined castle, conspirators, baffled plotters, a close call, and the colonel's warning, with Marshal Foch and General Pershing appearing.

German rioting, a trail, a bare chance, a trap door, a perilous situation, and turning the tables follow, with the claws of the Huns, squaring accounts, and the treaty signed. Frank Sheldon and Bart Raymond open the tale doubting the looks of things. Randall writes occupation duty as boy adventure with real stakes.
61711-pig-raising-a-manual-for-pig-clubs:
Aretas W Nolan and James H Greene wrote Pig Raising, a manual for pig clubs, issued by Row, Peterson and Company in Chicago and New York in nineteen eighteen. Nolan taught farm extension at the University of Illinois. Greene led junior extension work in that state. The book is in three parts. A pig raising calendar stands first, and hands on exercises stand second.

Exercises treat wild kin of swine, swine on the home farm, and market prices. Boys learn to judge pigs, weigh them with steelyards, and build troughs and hurdles. Part three treats breeds, bacon type and lard type hogs, and the choice of pigs. Care, houses, sanitation, worms, hog cholera, and feeds fill later heads. Club boys got a full course from first pig to market day. Farm families can still use much of the plain advice.
62254-fabiola-or-the-church-of-the-catac:
Fabiola, or The Church of the Catacombs, is a tale of the early church by Cardinal Wiseman. This illustrated edition was printed in 1886 by Benziger Brothers of New York, Cincinnati, and Saint Louis. A preface by Father Brennan of Saint Rose of Lima's Church in New York opens the volume. A picture of Saint Agnes stands at the front.

The title page calls the book a historical picture of the sufferings of the early church in pagan Rome. It sets out the glories of the martyrs through lives such as Agnes the fair young virgin and Sebastian the heroic soldier. Wiseman wrote the tale in scraps of leisure time, in inns and strange houses, as its own preface tells.
63956-queen-of-the-martian-catacombs:
Leigh Brackett wrote a Mars tale printed in the magazine Planet Stories in the summer of 1949. A cover note tells of a gaunt giant and a proud beauty crossing red sands, half mad with thirst. One of them knows a place where cool water laps old stones, a place of secret dread that means death to reveal.

The tale opens as a riders worn beast gives out in the lee of a sand hill. Four black shapes race up behind him across the waste, and safety at a town called Valkis lies past a far ridge he cannot reach. He makes instead for a lone rock tower, set on fighting there on foot.
64225-the-story-of-mrs-tubbs:
The Story of Mrs. Tubbs is a tale for the young, told and drawn by Hugh Lofting. It was put out at New York in nineteen twenty three. The front plate shows the dame of the name at the age of one mint years. The book is sworn to two maids of one name. The tale starts in the old form of the fair tale: once past a time.

Once past a time, long, long years past, there lived a most old dame, the tale says. Her name was Tubbs, and she lived on a small farm far in the wilds. Her small house stood at the edge of the woods. It was not far from a town with a small church. A small stream with a small bridge past it flow by the house.
65967-the-history-of-silk-cotton-linen-w:
The History of Silk, Cotton, Linen, Wool and Other Fibrous Substances, published at New York in 1845, tells the story of cloth and the arts behind it. Harper and Brothers printed it with steel engravings, and it is inscribed to the people of the United States. Chapters treat spinning, dyeing and weaving, and the pastoral life of the ancients.

The preface complains that history records crimes and battles, not useful arts. Long ages of peace, when skills were perfected, get a bare line and pass. The writer would trade a hundred ancient sieges for one lost art. Appendices take up Pliny's natural history, the origin of linen and cotton paper, felting and netting. Chinese looms appear in the first plate.
65975-the-making-of-a-man-being-a-descri:
The Making of a Man is a maker's guide to artificial limbs, issued by the George R Fuller Company of Rochester, New York, and copyrighted in 1902. Branches at Buffalo and Philadelphia are listed on the title page. The subtitle states the aim plainly: how such limbs may be adopted by those who have suffered loss of their natural limbs.

The introduction argues that exercise and physical work should be open to all, and that modern surgery and device-making now let the limbless share them. Peter Stuyvesant, who lost a leg in 1640 and pegged through life, stands as the old way's emblem.
66184-his-royal-nibs:
Winifred Eaton Reeve wrote His Royal Nibs, a novel put out in New York in 1925. Reeve had also written a tale called Cattle. She gave this book to Carl Laemmle, with her warm praise. The tale opens on the Banff road, in dust, heat, and noise.

Cars rush past and give no lift to men on foot that year. Most of those men are old troops in search of work. They plod from Calgary to wood camps, road camps, and ranches in the hills. Their hopes, fed by smooth talk in England, prove false in most cases. The O Bar O ranch sits on a hill half way to Banff. Its white and green sheds view all the land round it, and the tale settles there.
67368-sam-in-the-suburbs:
Sam in the Suburbs is a comic novel by Wodehouse of Sam and Valley Fields. George Doran of New York issued the book in nineteen twenty five. It first ran in Curtis papers that same year in serial form. Wodehouse also wrote Bill the Conqueror and Leave It to Psmith then.

Sam starts on a journey, then meets Kay of Valley Fields early on. Sailors do not care, a night club scene, and a coffee stall affair follow. Sam settles at San Rafael and Mon Repos and becomes a householder there. A syndicate, the dog Amy, and Lord Tilbury ally fill the middle chapters. Soapy Molloy busy afternoon and the missing millions close the romp.
69669-messalina-of-the-suburbs:
Delafield wrote Messalina of the Suburbs, published by Hutchinson in London. Her dedication letter, dated August 1923, explains the book's design. Causes, she and her friend had often agreed, are more interesting than the most dramatic results. So she reconstructs the inner developments that led, by inexorable degrees, to a catastrophe of murder. Such things, she writes, are never bolts from the blue; the real issue lies where personalities deserve dissection.

Her subject is Elsie Palmer. The novel opens with a mother's scolding: she will not have Elsie going with boys, and contradiction is the height of bad manners. Elsie denies, the mother knows a lie when she hears one, and the girl's crocodile tears earn no mercy. Delafield, later famous for her Provincial Lady diaries, here writes a tragedy of suburban respectability, tracing step by step how a girl of the suburbs reaches murder.
7018-a-collection-of-scotch-proverbs:
Scotch proverbs gathered by Pappity Stampoy in 1663 appear here with an introduction by Archer Taylor. General editors from Michigan, California, and other universities frame the volume, with assistant and advisory editors from Duke, Princeton, Columbia, and Chicago among them. The scholarly apparatus marks this as a modern reprint of a seventeenth century gathering.

The proverbs themselves preserve Scots speech, wit, and worldly wisdom in short, sharp sayings. Taylor's introduction sets Stampoy's haul in the history of proverb collecting. The book serves readers of Scots language, folk wisdom, and the plain talk of an older Scotland.
71927-a-visit-to-the-roman-catacombs:
J Spencer Northcote, provost of Birmingham, wrote A Visit to the Roman Catacombs. The S Anselm's Society published it at London in 1891. His preface traces a lifetime with the subject. His study began in 1846, and letters in the Rambler followed two years later. A small volume came in 1856, with a second edition in 1859. Then De Rossi's great work of 1864 and 1867 changed everything.

De Rossi added whole fields of detail and rebuilt the history under them. The old idea, that Christians buried underground for secrecy alone, fell away. Their cemeteries stood protected by law, like their pagan neighbors' burial places. Northcote's 1859 manual was thus shown incomplete and incorrect at once. A larger volume with W R Brownlow followed in 1869, on the new basis.
74014-lawrence-and-the-arabs:
Robert Graves wrote Lawrence and the Arabs, first published at London in nineteen twenty-seven. Eric Kennington edited the pictures and drew a bust of Lawrence for the front. Herry Perry made the maps.

Graves writes of his friend as Lawrence, the name he first knew him by. Friends, he notes, now call him by his initials, which at least seem fixed. Plates show the Emir Feisal, Feisal's army entering Wejh, and the ride to Akaba. Graves tells of the Arab revolt, the pilgrim railway, and raids that cut it. The book made Lawrence's war fame plain to home readers soon after the events.
74033-omnibuses-and-cabs:
Henry Charles Moore wrote Omnibuses and Cabs, Their Origin and History, with thirty-one illustrations. Chapman and Hall published it at London in 1902. Moore thanks George A Glover for early history and rare pictures, many printed here for the first time. He thanks G A Thrupp, the historian of coach-building, for his collection as well. The first part treats omnibuses, from the French carrosses a cinq sous onward.

The word omnibus gets its own inquiry, and Laffitte's Paris omnibuses follow. George Shillibeer brought the omnibus to England and ran the first route. His conductors defrauded him, and his anti-fraud plans failed to save him. He ran omnibuses against a railway, was ruined, and became an undertaker. Steam omnibuses, the Autopsy and the Automaton among them, failed in their turn. Twopenny and penny fares close the early story.
74916-weather-proverbs:
Weather Proverbs is number 9 in the Signal Service Notes of the War Department, printed in Washington in 1883. The booklet was prepared under Hazen, chief signal officer of the army, by Dunwoody, a lieutenant of artillery. A note asks all readers to send in popular weather sayings not in the set, so the collection may be made as complete as it can be.

The note is careful to add that the office forecasts rest not on proverbs but on observations accepted by weather science. Part one sorts sayings by animals, birds, clouds, dew, fish, fog, frost, insects, moon, plants, rain, rainbows, stars, snow, sun, thunder, trees, and wind. Part two treats instrument signs of storms, drawn from reports sent in from across the country.
75427-the-incredible-slingshot-bombs:
Robert Moore Williams wrote The Incredible Slingshot Bombs, a tale in Amazing Stories in May nineteen hundred forty two. A mere slingshot hurls more death than a thousand pound bomb, the head note warns. Tommy Britten, taunted as Tommy Sonofagun, holds the strange weapon. Ben Hopper, editor of the Summit Press, tells the tale.

Bloodhounds bay in Ten Mile Valley as the story opens. Sheriff Tim Hoskins hunts Tommy with his arm in a bloody sling. Tommy crossed a creek and threw the pack off his trail. Loafers at Brock’s Tavern taught the slow boy his mocking name. War fears guard the great power line on the ridge. Enemy agents might strike the high line, men feared then. Where Tommy got his deadly pellets forms the core riddle.
75848-hearts-and-clubs:
Amy Blanchard wrote Hearts and Clubs, a comedy in three acts published at Philadelphia in 1913. The cast is small and pointed: an elderly gentleman with a hobby, his nephew Tom Bestman, and a gentleman fond of his club. A spinster who adores beauty and Emerson leads the ladies.

The ladies of a local club take up physical culture, with a teacher and two advocates, one stout and one thin. The first scene is a seaside hotel sitting room, where a wife who fancies herself an invalid sighs on a sofa. Her husband prescribes distraction and music downstairs. The whole piece plays in about an hour and a quarter. Parlour actors of the day got a light comedy of clubs, culture, and hearts.
76579-the-strange-transfiguration-of-han:
Florence Marryat wrote The Strange Transfiguration of Hannah Stubbs, a novel put out in London in 1896. A line from Hamlet heads the book, on things in heaven and earth past our dreams. Marryat had told tales of a clash of love and of her own child. Twenty parts, with no names but their marks, make up the book.

The tale opens at a house of rooms in Soho, run by a Mrs Battleby. A brass plate by the bell names Signor Ricardo, a teacher of the tongue of Italy. Ricardo is all that is good in the eyes of his landlady, save that he is a riddle. He is tall and thin, with hawk keen grey eyes and a pointed beard. He is a poor exile whose lands were seized for a fault of state.
8020-the-bible-king-james-version-book-2:
The proverbs of Solomon, son of David, open this collection with its purpose stated plainly: to know wisdom, receive instruction, and give the young knowledge and discretion. The book gathers short sayings on speech, money, work, friendship, anger, and drink, contrasting the wise with the fool in couplet after couplet. Longer passages praise Lady Wisdom, who calls in the streets, and warn against the seductress and the sluggard.

Proverbs is the Bible's handbook for everyday conduct, practical rather than theological. Its lines are short enough to remember and sharp enough to sting, which is why so many have entered common speech. In the King James Version, its balanced phrases make it a book to read a little at a time, and to return to across a lifetime.
8247-the-world-english-bible-web-proverb:
Proverbs gathers short, sharp sayings meant to teach young people how to live wisely in ancient Israel. Much of it is linked to Solomon, famed for wisdom, though the book itself collects advice from several hands. Two paths run through it: wisdom, pictured as a woman calling in the streets, and folly, which leads to ruin. Honest work, careful speech, and respect for parents recur again and again.

The sayings are built to be remembered, often in paired lines that contrast the wise and the foolish. Later chapters add the words of other sages and a praise of a capable wife who runs a household with skill. Readers use Proverbs as a handbook of conduct, dipping in for one saying at a time rather than reading straight through.
a-collection-of-scotch-proverbs:
Pappity Stampoy collected his Scotch proverbs in 1663, and this modern scholarly printing adds an introduction by Archer Taylor, a leading student of the proverb. The title page lists the book's editors from the universities of Michigan, California, and elsewhere, a sign of how seriously the little book is now taken. Stampoy's was among the earliest printed gatherings of Scottish sayings.

The proverbs run in the speech of their time, on thrift, weather, wives, neighbors, ministers, and luck, each a sentence of folk judgment sharpened by use. Taylor's introduction places the collection in the history of proverb books. Readers meet old Scotland thinking aloud, canny, funny, and often severe, in lines made to be quoted.
a-description-of-modern-birmingham-where: Charles Pye describes modern Birmingham with observations from an excursion round the town in the summer of 1818. The account takes in Warwick and Leamington as well as Birmingham itself. Pye, who compiled a dictionary of ancient geography, writes for readers and travelers. The book gives a lively picture of an industrial town in the early nineteenth century.
a-handbook-for-latin-clubs: Susan Paxson gives a handbook for Latin clubs in schools. Its programs treat the value of Latin, Pompeii, ancient Rome, the forum, the Roman house, slaves, children, and education. Later programs cover doctors, soldiers, Caesar, and Cicero. Paxson, a teacher of Latin in Omaha, designed the book for club meetings and class use.
army-boys-on-german-soil-our-doughboys-q: Homer Randall's Army Boys novel follows Frank Sheldon and Bart Raymond, American doughboys stationed at Coblenz on the Rhine after the Great War. Flashes from guns, a ruined castle, conspirators and German rioting test the boys as they trail plotters, raise trap doors and face perilous situations. Marshal Foch and General Pershing appear before the treaty is signed and accounts are squared.
britannica-1911-arabs:
Arabs is the name given to that branch of the Semitic peoples of the Arabian peninsula, as this 1911 Britannica article explains. From the earliest historic times they lived in its south-western portion. In a narrow sense the name first covered only the nomad tribes ranging the north of the peninsula. Before the Christian era it had come to cover all the people of the peninsula.

By the time of the article, Arabs lived besides in Arabia across parts of Mesopotamia and the west shores of the Red Sea. They also lived on the east coast of the Persian Gulf and in the north of Africa. It picks out the Arabs of south Arabia and the Bedouin of the inner desert as the finest type of the stock. Coastal and town Arabs, it says, show mixing with other peoples.
britannica-1911-caribs:
The Caribs were a South American people of the Caribbean. Columbus first used their name, from Cariba. That word was said to mean “a valiant man.” This 1911 Britannica article examines their home and history. At the Spanish arrival they held parts of Guiana. They also held the lower Orinoco and the Windward Islands. Their original home was once placed in North America.

That view has been abandoned, the article says. German explorers found archaic Carib tribes in central Brazil. The Bakairi and Nahuquas speak an old type of Carib speech. So the cradle of the race was central South America. Their warlike resistance to the Spaniards was stout. They were cannibals, and the word comes from their name. Columbus's Caribal turned into Cannibal in European mouths. The article describes their slight build and their habits. Heavy drinking of cassava liquor marked their feasts.
britannica-1911-cubebs:
Cubebs are the fruit of several species of pepper, plants of the order Piperaceae. The drug of pharmacy comes from Piper Cubeba, a climbing woody shrub of south Borneo, Sumatra, and Java. Its berries grow forty or fifty to a stem and are picked before they ripen, then carefully dried. The dried berry is grey-brown and wrinkled, with a hard, white, oily seed. Its smell is pleasant and aromatic, and its taste is pungent and lasting.

Distilling cubebs gives about 15 percent of a volatile oil, the form in which the drug is most used. The entry lists its parts, from cubebene and camphor of cubebs to cubebin, found in 1839. The drug acts as a strong diuretic and can raise a skin rash as it leaves the body. A kin species yields the African cubebs traded from the Grain Coast in the 1300s.
britannica-1911-plebs: Plebs is a short Roman history entry from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The word comes from a root tied to fullness, like the Latin plenus. It names the multitude, the class with no special rights in the early Roman state, a bar that at first rested on birth. After the two orders won equal standing in law, the name covered the lower classes at large. Under the empire it was used, as a rule, for the city poor.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-caribs:
The Caribs were probably the second most numerous Indigenous stock of South America. A partly nomadic people, they ranked below the settled peoples of Peru and Bolivia in number. They were the second group Columbus met in the Antilles, where their name already meant cannibals to Europeans. At that time they held all the Lesser Antilles and raided the Arawaks of the larger islands, killing men and carrying women away as slaves.

Hardy sailors who paddled long distances between islands, they fought with weapons better than the fire-hardened javelins and wooden clubs of the Greater Antilles. They differed little from Arawaks in dress and dwellings, wore their hair long where Arawaks cut it short, and spoke a wholly different language. Their proper name is Karina. Language study points to an original home on the upper Shingu in Brazil, from which they spread north driving the Arawaks before them.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-proverbs:
Proverbs, one of the wisdom books of the Old Testament, stands in the Hebrew Bible among the Writings. In the Vulgate it sits just after Psalms and Job. This encyclopedia entry opens with its names. The Hebrew heading is Mishle Shelomoh, Proverbs of Solomon, shortened in Jewish use to Mishle. Greek and Latin forms of those titles gave the book its familiar name. Its sayings aim to teach practical wisdom for daily conduct.

Much of the entry weighs the ancient versions, above all the Septuagint. That Greek rendering was probably made in the middle of the second century BC. It differs from the Hebrew Masoretic text in omissions, rearrangements and additions. Its translator sometimes paraphrased where terse Hebrew sayings resisted a plain Greek turn. Later sections treat the book's structure and the standard commentaries, from Toy to Kent and Davison, for readers studying biblical wisdom literature.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-roman-catacom:
Roman catacombs are treated in this entry under seven heads: position, history, inscriptions, paintings, sarcophagi, small objects found, and catacombs outside Rome. Rome's soil is volcanic, with alluvial deposits only on the Tiber's right bank. Three strata appear: pozzolano on top, tufa in the middle, half earth and half stone, and solid stone below.

The lowest layer was quarried from earliest times. Every catacomb lies in the middle tufa, which yielded no building stone. Narrow straight passages with vertical walls differ plainly from quarry galleries. Sometimes a sandpit gave the starting point, letting Christians enter the city of the dead unnoticed in persecution. Stairways drop thirty-three to forty-nine feet or more to galleries ten to thirteen feet high. Barely wide enough for two grave-diggers carrying a bier, they branch into side passages and lower levels, some with three or four stories, as at St Sebastian.
guide-to-life-and-literature-of-the-sout:
J. Frank Dobie, the Texas folklorist and teacher, wrote his Guide to Life and Literature of the Southwest in 1943 and later enlarged it. Dobie set out to map the books that record the Southwest he loved: Texas and the border lands, the plains, the deserts, and the Spanish and Mexican centuries beneath them. Chapter by chapter he sorts writings on ranch life, cattle trails, Indians, outlaws, treasure tales, and folk song.

Dobie is no dry cataloguer. He praises, scolds, and tells stories as he goes, steering young readers toward the strong books and warning them off the fakes. The guide grew from his famous university course and remains a doorway into the region's letters, written by a man who had ridden much of the ground himself.
hardy-ornamental-flowering-trees-and-shr:
A. D. Webster, author of Practical Forestry, wrote Hardy Ornamental Flowering Trees and Shrubs to reform British planting. His preface, dated 1893 in this 1897 printing, states the object plainly. Planters repeat the same trees in nine-tenths of parks and gardens: elms, limes, and oaks. Among shrubs they repeat cherry laurel and privet. This sameness, he argues, is neither necessary nor desirable. A host of choice flowering species, he argues, is hardy and easy, yet little known.

Plant by plant, the book describes those species, with their habits, seasons, and culture. Webster writes as a working forester, not a parlor botanist. His plea is for variety and for flowers in public plantings. The book helped change the look of British parks, and it still serves any planter who wants bloom beyond the laurel hedge.
podcast-dannyjones-IMFvB1_2wbs:
Geologist Randall Carlson and researcher Ben Van Kerkwyk join Danny Jones to explore ancient earth's most violent catastrophes. They discuss impacts, floods, and firestorms. In their account, such events smashed early human civilization and were remembered worldwide as myth.

Randall Carlson has argued for decades that a comet strike reset human history at the end of the last ice age. Mainstream geology has partly warmed to that claim and partly resisted it. Van Kerkwyk adds the field evidence from sites they have visited together. Jones plays the informed amateur, asking for the strongest proofs. The episode is a seminar in catastrophism from its leading popularizers. Listeners can follow the geological argument in detail and judge where it converges with, and where it departs from, the textbooks.
podcast-joerogan-hwRD0NvAnbs:
Paul Stamets is back with Rogan for episode 2347 of the Joe Rogan Experience, with more mushrooms in hand. Stamets, the mycologist who never tires of his subject, treats each visit as a new dispatch from the fungal world. His enthusiasm is the show's renewable resource.

He and Rogan range across mycelium networks, mushroom medicine, and the mind-bending finds his field keeps producing. Rogan feeds him the questions of a fascinated amateur. The episode is a feast for the myco-curious, proof that one man's life work, retold with joy, can hold an audience through many returns to the same rich ground.
podcast-joerogan-yq0TP6WpyBs:
An animated short gives Joe Rogan's DMT tale the JRE Toon treatment. The file is not a full talk but a cartoon cut of a famed bit from the show. Rogan's voice tells the trip tale while the art plays it out.

Rogan tells of the blast, the elves, and the jester-like beings of his most told trip. The toon form makes the wild tale light and quick. Fans of the show know the bit by heart and quote it often. Listeners get a fun, short gem from the show's vault. The library holds the file as an archive record of the short.
tanakh-jps-1917-proverbs:
Proverbs is a wisdom book of the Hebrew Bible, presented in the 1917 Jewish Publication Society translation. It is headed as the proverbs of Solomon son of David, king of Israel, given to teach wisdom and sound judgment.

The first chapter states the aim: to give prudence to the simple and wise counsel to the old and young alike. Fear of the Lord is called the start of knowledge, while fools scorn good sense. A father then warns his son not to join gangs that lie in wait for blood and loot. Readers get short, sharp sayings on work, speech, wealth, and family life, long used as a guide for daily conduct.
the-bible-king-james-version-book-20-pro:
Proverbs in the King James text, starts as the proverbs of Solomon, son of David, king of Israel. Its aims are stated in a chain: to know wisdom and instruction, to perceive words of understanding, and to receive justice, judgment, and equity.

Simple readers gain subtlety, and the young gain knowledge and discretion, the verses say. A wise man will hear and increase learning. Fear of the Lord is called the beginning of knowledge, while fools despise instruction. A son is urged to hear his father's instruction and not forsake his mother's law, and to refuse when sinners entice him.
the-book-of-snobs:
William Makepeace Thackeray wrote The Book of Snobs, billed as the work of one of the snobs themselves. In his first remarks he sets out to prove that a book on snobs is a true need of the age. He claims the world has been getting ready for both the work and the man. Snobs, he says, are to be studied like any part of nature, and they run through all ranks.

His proof is a romp through great names and small ads. When France had to be dosed, he jokes, Robespierre was at hand, a foul dose the land drank with zest. When John Bull had to be kicked out of America, Washington stepped up. When a lord fell ill, a pill man cured him, at least in the ads. Thackeray mocks each new plan that claims the world cried out for it.
the-minds-and-manners-of-wild-animals-a-: William T. Hornaday, director of the New York Zoological Park, published The Minds and Manners of Wild Animals in May 1922, a book of personal observations. Only the title pages, an illustration caption, the dedication, and the opening contents are present here, so the text itself does not appear. A caption describes a lava ram in the Pinacate Mountains standing spellbound for twenty minutes before two men and a pack mule. Hornaday dedicated the volume to his park's officers and men, whose safety depends on knowing wild animals' minds.
the-women-of-the-arabs: Title pages and a dedication are what appear for The Women of the Arabs, entered for copyright in 1873. Rev. Henry Harris Jessup wrote it after seventeen years as an American missionary in Syria. Rev. C. S. Robinson and Rev. Isaac Riley edited the volume. Dodd and Mead published it in New York. A Mount Lebanon proverb about daughters stands as an epigraph. Jessup dedicates the book to the Christian women of America.
the-world-english-bible-web-proverbs:
Book twenty in the World English Bible collects the proverbs of Solomon, David's son. Their purpose is stated right away: to know wisdom and instruction. Young readers gain prudence, knowledge, and discretion. Wise readers hear and increase in learning. Understanding proverbs and riddles is another stated goal. Then comes the book's foundation line about fearing God.

Reverence for God is knowledge's beginning, Solomon says. Fools despise wisdom and instruction instead. A father's teaching and a mother's guidance form a garland, he adds. Sinners may entice, but the son must not consent. Short sayings on money, speech, and diligence follow for thirty-one chapters.
